justice: Pedestrian space is not clearly allocated: there is no marked sidewalk, and the walking area appears to be the same narrow edge used by vehicles, indicating weak equity in space distribution across users
Accessibility is limited by edge obstacles and uneven margins: tree bases, planted strips, and irregular curb edges reduce continuous, predictable passage for all users
Roadside parking (vans/cars occupying the edge) effectively reallocates public space toward drivers and away from people walking or cycling, reducing fairness of access to the corridor
safety: The street is narrow with two-way vehicle presence and roadside parking, creating pinch points that increase conflict risk between vehicles and pedestrians/cyclists
No visible crosswalks, centerline, or traffic-calming markings/signage are present, reducing driver guidance and increasing uncertainty for all road users
Overhead utility lines and poles indicate cluttered roadside infrastructure; combined with limited clear refuge space at the edges, this reduces perceived and functional safety for people walking
livability: Street frontage is dominated by blank walls/fences with limited active ground-floor uses, reducing natural surveillance and everyday street vitality
Lack of visible public amenities (benches, small plazas, lighting fixtures) suggests limited support for lingering or social interaction along the corridor
Some greenery exists (street-edge trees/shrubs), but it is sparse and not organized into a comfortable public realm, limiting the street’s recreational/neighborly appeal
sustainability: Existing trees and shrubs provide some ecosystem service potential (shade, air quality), though canopy coverage is limited
Strong reliance on private vehicles is suggested by multiple parked vehicles along the street, indicating weaker support for low-carbon mobility
No visible green stormwater features (rain gardens/permeable paving) are apparent; the roadway surface looks largely impervious asphalt/concrete
aesthetics: Visual clutter from dense overhead wires and multiple utility poles reduces streetscape coherence
Long, plain boundary walls and mismatched building edges create a monotonous and enclosed feel with limited architectural interest
Some greenery softens the scene, but inconsistent planting and hard-edged boundaries limit overall visual quality
comfort: Thermal comfort is limited: tree canopy is sparse and does not provide continuous shade along the walking edge
Physical comfort is low due to the absence of a defined, level sidewalk and the presence of edge irregularities (curb/planting strip/tree bases) that constrain walking space
Psychological comfort is reduced by close proximity to moving/parked vehicles in a narrow corridor, with little separation or buffer between people and traffic
walkability: No continuous, clearly separated sidewalk is visible; pedestrians likely share the carriageway edge with vehicles, reducing walking suitability
Roadside parking and narrow effective width force frequent yielding and detours, breaking walking continuity
Limited streetscape support elements (marked crossings, pedestrian lighting, wayfinding) reduce walking clarity and comfort for all users
bikeability: There are no bike lanes, markings, or physical protection; cyclists must mix with motor vehicles in a narrow street
Roadside parked vehicles create door-zone and weaving hazards, especially where the travel path narrows near vans/cars
Lack of intersection/priority cues (lane lines, signage) and constrained sightlines along a walled corridor reduce cycling predictability and comfort
